seoTitle: How to Find and Use the Heatmap Feature in TradingView
metaDescription: Learn how to locate the TradingView Heatmap under Products, switch between Stock and Crypto views, and read its color-coded sector layout at a glance.
intro: The TradingView Heatmap turns hundreds of tickers into a single color-coded grid, so you can tell which sectors or coins are moving without scanning a list one row at a time. This guide shows exactly where the Heatmap lives in TradingView's menu, what a real Stock Heatmap and Crypto Heatmap look like once you open them, and how to read the size and color of each box. It also covers switching asset classes and where the Heatmap fits next to TradingView's other market tools.

steps.heading: Open the Products menu
steps.body: From the TradingView homepage, click Products in the top navigation bar rather than Markets — this is where the Heatmap and related tools actually live, grouped under Individual Tools alongside Screeners, Calendars, News Flow, Portfolios, Yield Curves, Options, and Fundamental Graphs. Supercharts sits at the top of this same menu as the main charting terminal, but for a market-wide visual overview, the Heatmap is the one you want.

image.caption: TradingView's Products menu open, listing Supercharts at the top and Individual Tools like Screeners, Calendars, and Fundamental Graphs underneath.

steps.heading: Land on the Stock Heatmap
steps.body: Selecting the Heatmap tool opens the Stock Heatmap, defaulted here to the S&P 500 Index. The whole screen is a grid of colored rectangles grouped into labeled sectors — Electronic Technology, Technology Services, Retail Trade, Health Technology, Finance, and more — with each rectangle's size representing that company's relative market cap and its color showing daily performance, red for down and green for up. Individual names like NVDA, AAPL, MSFT, META, and TSLA are large enough to read directly because they dominate their sectors by size; smaller constituents cluster into tighter grids within the same block.

image.caption: The Stock Heatmap for the S&P 500, sectors like Technology Services and Finance visible as labeled blocks, with box size tied to market cap and color to daily change.

steps.heading: Adjust what the size and color represent
steps.body: Three dropdowns sit right above the grid: the index selector (S&P 500 Index by default, swappable for other indices), a sizing control currently set to Market cap, and a coloring control set to Change D, %. Switching the sizing dropdown re-scales every box by a different metric, and switching the coloring dropdown changes what the red-to-green gradient actually represents — useful if you want to color by weekly or monthly change instead of the daily default. A Sector dropdown next to those controls how the grid is grouped in the first place.

steps.heading: Switch to the Crypto Coins Heatmap
steps.body: The same tool works for crypto — switching the asset class swaps the entire grid to Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, XRP, and the rest of the top coins by market cap, using the identical size-by-cap, color-by-change logic. In this view Bitcoin and Ethereum dominate the layout as expected, while smaller-cap coins compress into a dense grid in the corner, which is exactly the kind of at-a-glance scan that's tedious to do from a sorted table instead.

image.caption: The Crypto Coins Heatmap, Bitcoin and Ethereum sized largest by market cap, with smaller coins packed into a dense grid on the right.

steps.heading: Know when to reach for the Screener instead
steps.body: The Heatmap is built for pattern-spotting, not precision — it tells you at a glance that Technology Services is red today, but it won't hand you exact volume, P/E ratios, or custom multi-condition filters the way the Screener does. Reach for the Heatmap first to spot where the action is, then switch to the Screener to filter that sector or asset class down to a specific list you can actually act on. Treating them as sequential steps rather than competing tools is the more useful habit.

steps.heading: Check mobile and account-level access
steps.body: The Heatmap is available in the TradingView mobile app as well as the desktop site, under the same Markets-adjacent navigation, and works on a free account without any paid plan required for the core view. Premium plans add deeper Heatmap analytics and extra customization on top of the same base layout, so it's worth trying the free version first to see whether the additional detail is something you'd actually use.

faq.question: Where is the Heatmap feature in TradingView?
faq.answer: Open the Products menu in the top navigation and look under Individual Tools — the Heatmap sits alongside Screeners, Calendars, and Fundamental Graphs, separate from the main Markets tab.

faq.question: Is the TradingView Heatmap available on mobile?
faq.answer: Yes, the Heatmap can be accessed on both the desktop platform and the TradingView mobile app, with the same size-by-market-cap, color-by-change layout.

faq.question: What's the difference between the Heatmap and the Screener?
faq.answer: The Heatmap gives a quick color-coded visual of performance by sector or asset, while the Screener offers detailed, filterable data in list form — the Heatmap is for spotting where to look, the Screener for digging into specifics.

faq.question: Do I need a premium plan to use the Heatmap?
faq.answer: No, basic Heatmap access for both Stocks and Crypto Coins is available on a free account; premium plans unlock additional analytics and customization on top of the same view.

faq.question: Can I change what the Heatmap's colors and box sizes represent?
faq.answer: Yes, the dropdowns above the grid let you change the sizing metric from Market cap to something else and the coloring metric from daily change to a different time frame.
